Lunch with Leupp and Avery Andrews
Letter to Hay on Santo Domingo and peace feelers

letters.topic: Morales's request, Russo-Japanese peace interest, wishes for Hay's health

headline: The Kaiser lands in Morocco
summary: Kaiser Wilhelm visits Tangier and backs the Sultan of Morocco against France and Britain, alarming Europe. In Washington Roosevelt sees Jane Addams among other callers and writes about Edwin Arlington Robinson and Russo-Japanese peace talks, while Edith takes the children, minus Quentin, cruising on the Sylph in Florida.

events.detail: Cabinet meeting
Callers include Jane Addams, Jusserand, Elkins, Hepburn and H. B. F. Macfarland
Lunches with John Willis and his wife
Wilhelm II visits Morocco and pledges support to the Sultan
Letters to Gilder and Sternberg
Edith and most of the children cruise the St. Johns River on the Sylph

letters.topic: Edwin Arlington Robinson
Possible Russo-Japanese peace talks

uncertain: The record places the Kaiser's Morocco visit on this date, matching the usual dating of his landing at Tangier.

headline: A new Panama Canal Commission
summary: Roosevelt's reorganized Panama Canal Commission takes over, with Theodore Shonts as chairman, Charles Magoon governing the Canal Zone and John Findley Wallace as chief engineer. He also talks Nebraska patronage with Rep. Hinshaw and lunches with Shonts and journalists.

events.detail: Nebraska appointments with Rep. Hinshaw
Durand, Quesada and Sternberg call
Lunch with Shonts, O'Laughlin, Egan, Byrne and Chapin
Second Isthmian Canal Commission takes office
Writes Andrew Jackson Montague about the commission

letters.topic: Reorganizing the Panama Canal Commission

headline: Wrapping up before a long trip
summary: On the eve of a six-week trip west, Roosevelt meets Francis Loomis, sees Clement Griscom and the Spanish ambassador, dines at Lodge's, and sends John Hay a survey of affairs at home and abroad, defending action in Santo Domingo.

events.detail: Meets Loomis
Clement Griscom
Dinner at Lodge's
Spanish ambassador
Letter to Hay surveying affairs before his vacation

letters.topic: Santo Domingo and the state of affairs as he leaves

tr_quotes.text: I felt that much less trouble would come from action

headline: Off to hunt in the Southwest
summary: At nine in the morning Roosevelt leaves Washington to hunt in the Southwest, leaving Taft in charge at home. He writes Theodore Shonts about sanitation in Panama.

events.detail: Leaves Washington for the Southwest
Letter to Shonts on Panama sanitation

letters.topic: Sanitary conditions in Panama

headline: Speaking in Louisville
summary: Roosevelt's train heads west, with a speech in Louisville and stops in five states from Kentucky to Missouri.

events.detail: Speaks at Louisville
Halts in Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Missouri and Kentucky

headline: Through Indian Territory to Dallas
summary: Roosevelt speaks at Parsons, Kansas, and at Muskogee, South McAlester and Durant in Indian Territory, then arrives in Dallas in the evening for another speech. Sternberg writes that Germany wants French ambitions in North Africa checked.

events.detail: Speeches at Parsons, Muskogee, South McAlester and Durant
Evening arrival and speech in Dallas
Letter from Sternberg on Germany and North Africa

letters.topic: Germany wants French aims in North Africa restrained

headline: Texas legislature and San Antonio
summary: Roosevelt stops at Taylor, addresses the Texas Legislature in Austin and reaches San Antonio. His diary jots notes on the men he will hunt with, including wolf catcher Abernathy, who lifts a coyote by the jaw on horseback, and Burk Burnett.

events.detail: Stop at Taylor
Addresses the Texas Legislature
Reaches San Antonio
Diary notes on hunting companions

uncertain: Much of this entry is hard to read in the record; the diary fragments are too broken to quote.

headline: Rough Riders reunion in San Antonio
summary: Roosevelt joins a reunion of his Rough Riders in San Antonio, where the regiment had trained in 1898, and says how much he admires Texans. His diary sketches Abernathy, who takes wolves with his bare hands, Texas Ranger Captain McDonald, and the cattlemen of the Four Sixes brand.

events.detail: Attends the Rough Riders reunion
Diary notes on Abernathy, Captain McDonald and the Four Sixes ranchers

tr_quotes.text: There is much to admire in them
Abernethy the homesteader & wolf catcher; he catches them with hands; his grayhounds; they will hold but not kill a big wolf

uncertain: The record spells the wolf hunter both 'Abernethy' and 'Abernathy', and gives the Ranger captain as 'Macdonald'.

headline: Coyote hunt begins near Frederick
summary: After speeches in Fort Worth and Wichita, Roosevelt reaches Frederick, Oklahoma, and starts hunting at Cecil Lyon's ranch. Dogs catch the first coyote in a creek, and Alec Lambert rides well. He tells Taft he is handling Russia, Japan, Santo Domingo and Morocco just right.

events.detail: Speeches at Fort Worth and Wichita
Arrives at Frederick
Coyote coursing near Frederick with Cecil Lyon and Dr. Lambert
Letter to Taft

letters.topic: Praise for his handling of Russia, Japan, Santo Domingo and Morocco

tr_quotes.text: First coyote seized by dogs in creek. Alec Lambert's good riding.
You are handling everything just right.

uncertain: 'Wichita, Kansas' as printed; given the route, Wichita Falls, Texas, is possible.

headline: Headlong gallops after coyotes
summary: On Archie's eleventh birthday Roosevelt rides hard after coyotes from a camp in a bend of the Red River, on a Kiowa pony in the morning and a cow pony later. His hosts are old-style Texas cattlemen including Burk Burnett and Cecil Lyon. He writes Bamie about little Sheffield's ear trouble.

events.detail: Archie turns 11
Day of coyote chases, one run of four miles
Letter to Bamie

letters.topic: Worry over little Sheffield's ears

tr_quotes.text: Today we opened our hunt successfully, killing two coyotes as the result of several headlong gallops.
Beautiful camp; in bend of Big Red branch of Red River

uncertain: The diary's tally of the day's kill is hard to read in the record.

headline: A ten-mile chase
summary: Out with greyhounds and staghounds, Roosevelt's party takes a coyote after a three-mile run. In the afternoon comes an extraordinary ten-mile chase, and Abernathy captures the coyote alive with his hands, with Roosevelt one of the few riders there at the finish.

events.detail: Morning coyote run on a roan cutting horse
Afternoon ten-mile run; Abernathy takes the coyote alive

tr_quotes.text: In afternoon went out again; extraordinary 10 mile run

headline: Bobcats elude the hounds
summary: Camped on Deep Red Creek, Roosevelt is up before dawn for a morning hunt after bobcats that turns up nothing, and he rests in the afternoon.

events.detail: Fruitless morning hunt for bobcats
Rests in the afternoon

tr_quotes.text: Up before dawn. Spent morning with train hounds in fruitless hunt after bobcats. Nothing. Rested in afternoon.

headline: Six coyotes in a day
summary: With the chuck wagon along, the party rides southwest toward the Red River and kills six coyotes, losing only one after a seven-mile chase. A cowpuncher with nothing but a rope chases that one back for miles.

events.detail: All-day hunt with the chuck wagon toward the Red River

tr_quotes.text: Killed 6 coyotes. Only one unsuccessful chase.

headline: Last day of the coyote hunt
summary: Roosevelt is in at the death of two more coyotes, then rides back to Frederick, where he speaks before leaving for Colorado. His diary tallies the party's total. Sternberg reports that the Kaiser is pressing for an international meeting on Morocco.

events.detail: Morning hunt; two coyotes taken
Rides back to Frederick
Speaks at Frederick
Leaves for Colorado in the evening
Letter from Sternberg on a Morocco conference

letters.topic: The Kaiser seeks a conference on Morocco

tr_quotes.text: Hunted in morning. In at death of 2 coyotes.

uncertain: The diary counts are hard to read in the record; the April 14 letter gives 47 wolves for the whole party.

headline: Colorado speeches, and tales of Abernathy
summary: Roosevelt speaks at Trinidad, Pueblo and Colorado Springs and spends the night at Newcastle. He tells Kermit the hunting party took 47 wolves plus raccoons and rattlesnakes, and describes how Abernathy takes wolves alive. He also writes Garfield about the probes into Standard Oil and the Beef Trust.

events.detail: Speeches at Trinidad, Pueblo and Colorado Springs
Overnight at Newcastle
Letters to Kermit and Garfield

letters.topic: Worry for Bamie and Sheffield; the hunt's bag; Abernathy's method
Inquiries into the meat packers and Standard Oil

tr_quotes.text: thrusting his gloved hands down between their jaws so that they cannot bite.

headline: Into the Colorado high country
summary: Roosevelt rides about 20 miles from Newcastle with Philip Stewart, Dr. Alexander Lambert and guides John Goff and Jake Borah to Camp Roosevelt on East Divide Creek, with three horses, a Springfield rifle and some thirty hounds and terriers. Snow lies in drifts.

events.detail: Rides from Newcastle to camp with Stewart, Lambert, Goff and Borah
Bear hunt camp set up on East Divide Creek

tr_quotes.text: Rode about 20 miles to our camp on upper waters of East Divide Creek. Very comfortable.
Snow in drifts. High rugged country.

uncertain: Guide's name printed 'Jake Vorah' here and 'Jake Borah' on April 20.

headline: Shorty and the bobcat
summary: Roosevelt spends eleven hours in the saddle over rough ground. The dogs tree a bobcat, the bull terrier Shorty climbs nearly to it, and when it jumps the pack seizes it. A big glossy black bear is spotted.

events.detail: Eleven-hour ride; dogs tree and kill a bobcat
Sees a large black bear

tr_quotes.text: Rode for 11 hours, over exceedingly difficult country. Horses climb like cats; wonderful endurance.

headline: A 330-pound black bear
summary: With 26 hounds and four terriers Roosevelt follows a black bear through snowy canyons for nearly two hours. The bear refuses to tree and fights off the dogs, killing a terrier; Roosevelt breaks its hips at 60 yards and finishes it at 30. It weighs 330 pounds.

events.detail: Kills a black bear after a long chase through deep snow

tr_quotes.text: Got him after chase of 1 3/4 hours. 330 lbs. Stomach empty.

headline: Skip and Shorty, the fighting dogs
summary: Six hours in the snowdrifts turn up nothing. Roosevelt's diary praises the little terrier Skip, who loves to ride on horseback, and Shorty, the bull terrier mauled by the bear, who staggers back wagging his tail. He notes cranes, eagles, ravens and the first songbirds.

events.detail: Six-hour ride with no game
Records sandhill cranes, eagles, ravens, jays and spring songbirds

tr_quotes.text: Rode 6 hours, mostly in snowdrifts; saw nothing.

headline: Loeb visits camp
summary: Secretary William Loeb spends the night in camp. Roosevelt rides all day in the high mountains without seeing game, and records local talk about wolves, cougars and a trapper who took dozens.

events.detail: Loeb stays overnight
All-day ride in the mountains; no game
Notes on local wolves and cougars

tr_quotes.text: Loeb spent night.
Rode all day; in high mts. Saw nothing.

uncertain: Much of the diary entry is illegible.

headline: Snowbound, writing on Morocco
summary: Snow keeps the party in camp, and Roosevelt fills his diary with birds and small mammals. In letters he tells Ted about his guides, tells Taft the government should stay out of Morocco, wires Loomis that the U.S. will remain friendly with both France and Germany, and writes Lodge on Newfoundland fisheries.

events.detail: Lists song sparrow, flicker, pinyon jays, blue grouse, magpies, chipmunks and mice
Letters to Ted, Taft, Lodge and Sternberg; telegram to Loomis

letters.topic: His guides Goff and Borah, and Stewart and Lambert
Morocco, Venezuela and the Bowen controversy
Telegram: no commitments on Morocco
Newfoundland fishing rights
The Moroccan crisis

tr_quotes.text: Snowy. In Camp.
I do not feel that as a government we should interfere in the Morocco matter.

uncertain: Letter to Ted was mailed from Glenwood Springs.

headline: Skip bites a bobcat's tail
summary: More than ten hours in the saddle and on foot through belly-deep drifts end with the hounds treeing a bobcat. Stewart photographs it, Lambert shoots it with a revolver, and the little terrier Skip climbs thirty feet up the tree to bite its tail.

events.detail: Long day; bobcat treed and killed by Lambert
Stewart photographs the treed bobcat

tr_quotes.text: Stewart photographed it.

headline: Fever and a move to West Divide
summary: Roosevelt feels his old Cuban fever. The party moves camp to where Clear Creek meets West Divide, though the late cold season may have kept the bears denned up.

events.detail: Bout of the fever he caught in Cuba
Camp moves to the junction of Clear Creek and West Divide

tr_quotes.text: Cuban fever.

headline: A rest day in camp
summary: Roosevelt stays in camp and records guide Jake Borah's story of a 115-pound wolf his pack once held at bay before he shot it.

events.detail: Rest day in camp
Notes Borah's account of a big wolf

tr_quotes.text: Stayed in camp.

headline: A she-bear shot through the heart
summary: In an eleven-hour, forty-mile ride, four of them bucking snow, the pack jumps a yearling and its glossy dark mother. Lambert shoots the yearling in an aspen; Roosevelt drops the she-bear from a spruce with a shot through the heart.

events.detail: Long ride; Lambert takes a yearling, Roosevelt kills the mother bear

tr_quotes.text: I shot her dead through heart.
Stomach contained rosebuds.

headline: Another bear after twelve hours
summary: After twelve hours and more than thirty miles, Lambert shoots two yearlings with his revolver and the hounds tree their mother high in a spruce, where Roosevelt kills her. He notes what the bears had eaten. Sternberg writes that the Kaiser wants Roosevelt to nudge Britain toward harmony with Germany over Morocco.

events.detail: Kills a she-bear treed by the hounds; Lambert takes two yearlings
Examines the bears' stomach contents
Letter from Sternberg on Britain, Germany and Morocco

letters.topic: The Kaiser asks him to urge British-German accord on Morocco

tr_quotes.text: I broke her neck.

headline: Ranchmen come to watch
summary: A touch of fever keeps Roosevelt in camp while some twenty hard-riding ranchmen turn out hoping to see the President kill a bear. He writes Ethel about prairie girls and admits he is homesick for the family.

events.detail: Mild fever; stays in camp
Local ranchmen ride out to watch the hunt
Letter to Ethel from Divide Creek

letters.topic: Prairie girls; missing home

tr_quotes.text: Touch of fever. Stayed in camp.

headline: Cutting the trip short for peace
summary: Still feverish, Roosevelt stays in camp while Lambert has a big day of bear hunting. Sensing that Russia and Japan may reach an honorable settlement, he wires Taft that he will end his trip a week early.

events.detail: Fever keeps him in camp
Lambert's successful bear hunt
Telegram to Taft on Russo-Japanese peace prospects

letters.topic: Prospects for peace; will shorten his trip

tr_quotes.text: Fever. Stayed in camp.

uncertain: The diary's bear count and weights are hard to read in the record.

headline: Watching a tame kingbird
summary: Another feverish day in camp. Roosevelt describes a tame bee martin that stays near the buildings with a plaintive note, and a big field mouse in the ranch house.

events.detail: Fever; stays in camp
Observes a bee martin and a field mouse

tr_quotes.text: Bee martin, tame, stays round buildings, rather plaintive & pleasant note.

headline: Fever in camp again
summary: Roosevelt spends another day in camp with fever. It is his sister Corinne's 23rd wedding anniversary.

events.detail: Fever; stays in camp
Corinne's 23rd wedding anniversary

tr_quotes.text: Fever. Stayed in camp.

headline: Church in a schoolhouse; Edith finds Pine Knot
summary: Roosevelt goes to church in a little blue schoolhouse and wires Taft that he backs Japan's call for direct peace talks with Russia. In Virginia, Edith buys a small timbered house and five acres in Albemarle County for $195, calling it Pine Knot, a hideaway for the two of them.

events.detail: Church service at the little blue schoolhouse
Telegram to Taft supporting direct Russo-Japanese talks
Edith buys Pine Knot from Will Wilmer's Plain Dealing Farm

letters.topic: Endorses direct peace negotiations between Russia and Japan

tr_quotes.text: Church at little blue school house.
I emphatically agree with the Japanese view that there should be direct negotiations on all terms of peace between Russia and Japan.

uncertain: The record does not date Edith's purchase precisely; it is placed on this day.
